::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Why ker f defines only in homomorphism?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1910991/why-ker-f-defines-only-in-homomorphism), asked by [Ashu5765449](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/362764/ashu5765449) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-09-01; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Why kernel of any map can only be defined in group homomorphism, why can't we define it on simple map. Just simply clarify my query.
:::

If I understand your question correctly, you're asking: *Why is it important that $f$ be a homomorphism when defining its kernel?*

If $f \colon G \to H$ is any map between groups, you *could* call the inverse image of the identity in $H$ the “kernel” of $f$.  But it's only when $f$ is a homomorphism that $\ker f$ is a subgroup.  If it weren't a subgroup, it wouldn't be very useful in algebraic terms.

For instance (since you asked for an example), let $f\colon \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ be defined by $f(x) = x^2 - 4$.  The “kernel” of this map would be $\left\{-2,2\right\}$.  But this isn't a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}$; it's not closed under addition.
